However, this doesn’t mean your head doesn’t matter in cold weather. Insulating it is still a smart move—but only as part of a well-rounded approach to winter clothing. Don’t let a myth dictate your wardrobe choices. Let science guide your understanding.

pages.text: Q: Mom always said to wear a hat in the cold because we lose 80% of our body heat through our head. Is that true? pages.text: As expected, all the volunteers lost heat quickest when they initially entered the water. But the rest of the results debunk popular expectation. The volunteers whose heat loss came almost entirely from their heads (those who were fully submerged whilst wearing insulating clothing) lost only half as much heat as those whose heat loss came almost entirely from their bodies (the volunteers in swimming costumes with their heads poking out of the water). In other words, we don’t lose most heat from our heads. The results show that having your head immersed in cold water only adds 10% to your overall heat loss in a cold pool. And given that the head accounts for 7% to 9% of the body’s surface, that doesn’t seem excessive. [...] Before this trip I’d never spent much time thinking about how the body loses heat. I sleep in my middle-of-the-range sleeping bag, wearing all of my clothes – four pairs of trousers, three fleeces, two hats and waterproofs. But it’s still not enough. Mariano, our guide, sleeps outside the tent, with nothing but his super-thick sleeping bag to shelter him from the wind. He insists he prefers it that way, and doesn’t even bother wearing a hat. pages.text: Claim You lose half of your body heat through your head, making it the most important part of your body to cover in frigid temperatures. Origin The earliest reference of this comes from the U.S. Army Field Manual in the 1950s, which claims that “40% to 45% of body heat” is lost through the head. Since then, this has been a favorite bit of wisdom that Midwestern mothers and fathers repeat to their kids every winter. Facts This theory was revisited in 2006 and again in 2008. In the 2006 study, subjects were placed in cold water, sometimes with their heads above water and sometimes with their heads submerged. Scientists found that the head accounts for about 7% heat loss, which is proportional to the amount of skin that’s showing. [...] The 2008 study corroborated these findings, saying that about 7% to 10% of body heat is lost through the head. The reality is that the amount of heat lost from a given part of your body is relative to how much skin is showing. If it were true that half of your body heat exits through the head, then it’d mean that you lose roughly 20 times as much heat per square inch as every other part of the body. “If you don’t have a hat on, you lose heat through your head, just as you would lose heat through your legs if you were wearing shorts,” said Dr. Richard Ingebretsen in an interview with WebMD. “There’s really no such thing as ‘cold’ when you’re talking about the body. There’s always heat—it’s just a matter of keeping it in.”

pages.text: dexshell logo Site icon Search Login Cart 23. September 2022 # Do We Really Lose More Heat Through Our Heads? Many of us grew up hearing that 40 or even 50 percent of body heat escapes through the head. The advice was simple: wear a hat, or lose most of your warmth. The percentage is misleading, but the practical advice is not. Your head does not possess a unique ability to release an enormous fixed share of body heat. Like any other body region, however, it loses heat when exposed—and it is often one of the few areas left uncovered after we put on a jacket, gloves and winter footwear. So why can a cold head make the rest of us feel so uncomfortable, and what kind of protection is useful in cold, wet weather? Head losing more heat Credit DexShell Instagram Contributor [...] Heat loss depends on several factors, including exposed surface area, insulation, wind, moisture, air temperature and activity level. The head represents only a relatively small proportion of the body’s total surface area. When the whole body is equally exposed, it does not normally account for anything close to half of total heat loss. The familiar percentage therefore misses the real point. During cold-weather activity, most of the body is usually insulated by clothing while the head and face may remain partially exposed. Under those circumstances, the head can become a meaningful route of heat loss—not because it behaves differently from every other body part, but because it has been left without comparable protection.

answerStatements.text: The evidence does not support the claim that most body heat is lost through the head. In the experiment described, volunteers whose heat loss came almost entirely from the head lost only half as much heat as those whose loss came almost entirely from the body
Having the head immersed in cold water added only about 10% to overall heat loss, and the head makes up roughly 7% to 9% of the body's surface area, so this share is not disproportionate

The popular figure traces to a US Army manual saying 40 to 45 percent of body heat can be lost from an unprotected head. The AskHistorians discussion describes this as a flawed interpretation, though it notes the scalp's thin fat layer and rich blood supply do raise head heat loss somewhat

analysis.answer: The evidence does not support the claim that most body heat is lost through the head. In the experiment described, volunteers whose heat loss came almost entirely from the head lost only half as much heat as those whose loss came almost entirely from the body [1]. Having the head immersed in cold water added only about 10% to overall heat loss, and the head makes up roughly 7% to 9% of the body's surface area, so this share is not disproportionate [1]. The popular figure traces to a US Army manual saying 40 to 45 percent of body heat can be lost from an unprotected head. The AskHistorians discussion describes this as a flawed interpretation, though it notes the scalp's thin fat layer and rich blood supply do raise head heat loss somewhat [2].
